\section[adoptar]{adoptar — to adopt}

\label{lesson:ES-C748-adoptar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the son-in-law, then the Spanish for the daughter-in-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: adoptar}
\textbf{adoptar} — \textquotedblleft{}to adopt\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Adoptaron a una niña.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They adopted a little girl.}
\end{quote}

Also for pets and ideas: \emph{adoptar un perro}, \emph{adoptar una medida}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{adoptar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{adoptāre} \textquotedblleft{}to choose for oneself\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{optāre} \textquotedblleft{}to choose\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{adoptar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{adoptar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{adoptar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the son-in-law, then the Spanish for the daughter-in-law, then say \emph{adoptar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does adoptar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To adopt\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acoger]{acoger — to take in, to foster; to welcome}

\label{lesson:ES-C748-acoger}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the daughter-in-law, then the Spanish for to adopt.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acoger}
\textbf{acoger} — \textquotedblleft{}to take in, to foster; to welcome\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Acogieron a dos niños durante un año.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They fostered two children for a year.}
\end{quote}

Spelling: \emph{acojo}. \emph{Una familia de acogida} — a foster family.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{acoger} is inherited from a spoken Latin \emph{accolligere} (EtymDB), built on \emph{colligere} \textquotedblleft{}to gather\textquotedblright{}: to gather someone in.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the daughter-in-law, then the Spanish for to adopt, then say \emph{acoger} again

\section[la madrastra]{la madrastra — the stepmother}

\label{lesson:ES-C748-madrastra}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to take in, then the Spanish for adoption.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la madrastra}
\textbf{la madrastra} — \textquotedblleft{}the stepmother\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se lleva bien con su madrastra.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She gets on well with her stepmother.}
\end{quote}

Fairy tales give it a bad name; today people often say \emph{la mujer de mi padre}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{madrastra} is inherited from spoken Latin \emph{mātrastra} (EtymDB), built on \emph{māter} \textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{} with a belittling ending.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la madrastra}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la madrastra}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la madrastra}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to take in, then the Spanish for adoption, then say \emph{la madrastra} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la madrastra mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The stepmother\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el padrastro]{el padrastro — the stepfather; the hangnail}

\label{lesson:ES-C748-padrastro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for adoption, then the Spanish for the stepmother.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el padrastro}
\textbf{el padrastro} — \textquotedblleft{}the stepfather; the hangnail\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi padrastro me enseñó a nadar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My stepfather taught me to swim.}
\end{quote}

Also a hangnail beside a fingernail.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{padrastro} is usually traced to a spoken Latin \emph{patraster}, built on \emph{pater} \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{} with the belittling ending \emph{-aster}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
